clue.text: Country doing no harm deposing government

indicators.note: to depose is to remove from power, so the letter for the ruling body is thrown out

parts.note: benign means harmless
G is the standard abbreviation for government

explanation.surface: A peaceful nation overthrows its own rulers.
explanation.walkthrough: Take G out of BENIGN to leave BENIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Benin is a West African state, so it is an example of a country.

clue.text: Thwarted swimmer longed to enter northerly place to surf well

indicators.note: entering something means going inside it
in a down clue, heading north means reading upwards, so the word runs backwards

parts.note: you surf the web
to ache for something is to long for it
hale means healthy, well

explanation.surface: A frustrated surfer longing to catch waves somewhere up north.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place to surf' looks like a beach, but it is the internet; in a down entry 'northerly' means the word reads upwards.
explanation.definitionFit: A whale stranded on a shore cannot swim, so it is a swimmer whose progress has been thwarted.

clue.text: Tory's flipping spin — a Liberal's in the dark?

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the letters run the other way

parts.note: Con is short for Conservative, the Tory party
a spin is a turn
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: A Conservative changing his spin leaves a Liberal confused.
explanation.walkthrough: CON flips to NOC, then TURN, A, L. Nocturnal means active by night.
explanation.definitionFit: Nocturnal things happen or are active at night, that is, in the dark.

clue.text: Suitable place for Otto I in north-east

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: NE is the compass abbreviation
Ich is German for I, the word a German such as Otto would use

explanation.surface: Somewhere fitting in the north-east for a German emperor, Otto the First.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Otto I' reads like the emperor; instead it means the word a German says for I, which sits inside NE.
explanation.definitionFit: A niche is a position or role that suits someone exactly, a fitting place.

clue.text: I disagree with Lord who ran round motorway twice

indicators.note: twice tells the solver to write the finished piece out a second time
going round something means surrounding it, so one piece sits inside the other

parts.note: Sebastian Coe, the Olympic middle-distance runner, is now Lord Coe
M is the abbreviation for motorway, as in the M1
the same peer again, because the clue says twice
the same motorway again, because the clue says twice

explanation.surface: A disgruntled athlete's protest against a peer who jogged laps of the motorway.
explanation.walkthrough: The runner wraps round the road and the result is written out twice. 'Come, come!' is a mild old-fashioned protest.
explanation.definitionFit: The exclamation expresses mild reproach or objection, the way someone signals they do not accept what was said.

clue.text: Mixed drinks and case of champagne drunk by phoney

indicators.note: something drunk by another goes inside it

parts.note: cod means fake, as in cod Latin
ales are drinks

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters are kept

parts.note: first and last letters

explanation.surface: A cocktail party with drinks and a case of fizz quaffed by a fraud.
explanation.walkthrough: Cod is British slang for sham or mock, as in cod Latin; 'Mixed' looks like a description of the drinks but is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Coalesced means came together into one mass, so the parts were merged or mixed.

clue.text: Forced this person to take notice

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside

parts.note: the setter referring to themself
an ad is a notice, such as a small ad

explanation.surface: Someone was compelled to pay attention.
explanation.walkthrough: ME takes in AD: M(AD)E.
explanation.definitionFit: If you made someone do something, you forced or compelled them to do it.

clue.text: One's driven into a bottleneck in county town, with crowd hemming in Sierra

indicators.note: hemming in means enclosing on all sides

parts.note: Cork is an Irish county and its city
Sierra is S in the NATO phonetic alphabet
a crew is a gang or crowd

explanation.surface: A traffic jam in a county town as crowds surround a car.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bottleneck' suggests congested traffic, but here it is literal: the neck of a bottle. Cork is both an Irish county and its main city.
explanation.definitionFit: The spiral of a corkscrew is twisted into a cork in the bottle's neck to pull it out.

clue.text: Doctor upset water drops in cut

parts.note: MO is a medical officer

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so the word reads bottom to top

parts.note: dew is drops of water

explanation.surface: An upset doctor drips water into a cut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like a wound for the doctor to treat, but it is a verb, as with grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Mowed is the past tense of mow, to cut grass or crops with a blade.

clue.text: American state banks prepare to fire old leader, getting high-flying duo

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for American

indicators.note: banks here is a verb: to bank something is to line its sides, so one word encloses another

parts.note: a state or country is a land
to cock a gun is to ready it for firing
Gordon Brown, former UK prime minister

explanation.surface: A US state's banks sack a former boss in a story about a pair of fliers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Banks' looks like financial institutions but is a verb meaning lines or encloses. Gordon Brown led the UK as prime minister 2007-10.
explanation.definitionFit: Alcock and Brown made the first non-stop transatlantic flight in 1919, so they are literally a pair of aviators.

clue.text: Protecting nothing, Thatcher set out to be ruinous

indicators.note: protecting something means surrounding it, so one piece goes inside
out suggests the letters are disordered and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
O is zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Margaret Thatcher set out to ruin things while protecting nobody.
explanation.walkthrough: Thatcher was UK prime minister 1979-90; 'set out' looks like a phrase but 'out' is the signal for rearranging.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that costs the earth is hugely expensive, so it would be ruinous to buy.

clue.text: Junior medics in residence drinking milk before noon

indicators.note: before places the last piece after what came first, in reading order
something drinking takes another thing inside itself

parts.note: a home is a residence
to milk a situation is to exploit or use it
N is the abbreviation for noon

explanation.surface: Young doctors living in hospital have a glass of milk in the morning.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Milk' is a verb here, meaning exploit, not the drink.
explanation.definitionFit: Housemen is the British term for junior hospital doctors in their first posts.

clue.text: Familiar with outside bar I trashed

indicators.note: something trashed is wrecked, so its letters are thrown into a new order
bar here means except, so the named letter is left out

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written, the letter removed

explanation.surface: Someone knows the scene outside a pub they wrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bar' looks like a pub, but it means 'except': OUTSIDE without I leaves OUTSDE to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: To be used to something is to be accustomed to it, which is to be familiar with it.

clue.text: Dull brown, oddly cheesy top? You'd be a fool to wear it

definitions.text: You'd be a fool to wear it

parts.note: dun is a dull greyish-brown colour

indicators.note: oddly asks for the letters in odd-numbered places, first, third, fifth

parts.note: the first, third and fifth letters
a cap is a top or lid, and also a hat

explanation.surface: A fashion note about an unflattering brown hat with a cheesy look.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition plays on 'fool': the cap was put on a slow pupil, so wearing one marks you as a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A dunce's cap was a conical hat put on a pupil judged stupid, so whoever wears it is cast as a fool.

clue.text: Seeing red pants with extra zip

indicators.note: pants is British slang for rubbish, so the letters are rubbishy and must be reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone furious about trousers with an extra zip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pants' looks like trousers with a zip, but as British slang for 'rubbish' it signals a shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Energised means filled with vigour, which is what having more zip, or pep, means.

clue.text: Manager gets trophy after a season using this

indicators.note: after places one piece behind another in reading order

parts.note: Pep Guardiola, the football manager
per means a, as in once per year
a pot is slang for a trophy, a cup

explanation.surface: A football manager wins a cup at the end of a season.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Season' is the verb to add flavouring, not part of the sporting year. Pep Guardiola is the Manchester City manager.
explanation.definitionFit: A pepper pot is the shaker you use when seasoning food with pepper.

clue.text: Break bags I take once more

indicators.note: to bag something is to put it in a bag, so one piece goes inside another

parts.note: a rest is a break
taken as written

explanation.surface: A holiday spent packing things up again.
explanation.walkthrough: REST holds I: RES(I)T. To resit is to take an exam again.
explanation.definitionFit: To resit an examination is to sit it, or take it, a second time after failing.

clue.text: Very soppy, like a family film after son cheers up

indicators.note: after places one piece behind another in reading order

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for son

indicators.note: up in a down clue means reading from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: ta is British slang for thanks, or cheers
a U-rated film is suitable for all ages in Britain

explanation.surface: A sentimental verdict on a cheerful family movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Soppy' suggests sentimental, but it means soaking wet. U is the British certificate for a film suitable for all.
explanation.definitionFit: Saturated means soaked through, and soppy literally means very wet.

clue.text: Orchestra in auditorium with echo

parts.note: a concert hall is an auditorium
Echo is E in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An orchestra plays in a hall with a strong echo.
explanation.walkthrough: The Hallé is a Manchester-based symphony orchestra.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hallé is a famous English symphony orchestra founded in Manchester by Charles Hallé.

clue.text: Aid when driving in day time in Suffolk town

parts.note: D is the abbreviation for day

indicators.note: one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: Ipswich is the county town of Suffolk, in eastern England
T is the abbreviation for time

explanation.surface: A tip for a motorist making a day trip to Ipswich.
explanation.walkthrough: Ipswich is the county town of Suffolk, in eastern England.
explanation.definitionFit: A dip switch lowers a car's headlights to avoid dazzling oncoming drivers, a driving aid.

clue.text: I think we should set off fires

definitions.text: I think we should set off
definitions.meaning: first meaning: a suggestion to depart
second meaning: dismisses an employee, read as two words

explanation.surface: Someone suggests leaving and then lighting fires, or setting off fireworks.
explanation.walkthrough: Read as LETS GO, the second sense is an employer releasing staff.
explanation.definitionFit: Let's go proposes departure; lets go (someone) is a euphemism for dismissing a worker, matching fires.

clue.text: Pound in change picked up for Mark in A Coruña

indicators.note: picked up in a down clue means lifted, so the word reads upwards
one thing being in another means it sits inside it

parts.note: to edit is to change
L is the abbreviation for pound, from libra

explanation.surface: Changing pounds into euros for a trip to a Spanish city.
explanation.walkthrough: EDIT is turned to TIDE, then L goes inside. The tilde is the wavy mark over the n in Coruña.
explanation.definitionFit: The tilde is the accent written over the n in Coruña, a mark found in that very name.

clue.text: Engineers insulating electronic fuse's surface again

indicators.note: insulating means wrapping round, so the outer letters enclose the inner one

parts.note: RE is the Royal Engineers, a British Army corps
E is short for electronic, as in e-mail
to fuse things is to merge them

explanation.surface: Engineers wrap electrical fuses, which leads to talk of their surface.
explanation.walkthrough: RE goes round E to give REE, then MERGE. The 's stands for 'is', linking wordplay to definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To re-emerge is to come up or appear again, which is what surfacing again means.

clue.text: What Persian said without purpose the wrong way

indicators.note: going the wrong way means running backwards

parts.note: w/o is the abbreviation for without
an aim is a purpose

explanation.surface: An Iranian speaker talking aimlessly and backwards.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Persian' looks like a person from Iran; it is a Persian cat.
explanation.definitionFit: A Persian is a breed of cat, and miaow is the sound a cat makes.

clue.text: The Dandy or its rival's not half posh

indicators.note: not half means only half is kept and the rest dropped

parts.note: The Beano was the Dandy's great rival among British children's comics
U means upper-class

explanation.surface: A comparison of two British comics, one apparently rather posh.
explanation.walkthrough: The Dandy and The Beano are long-running British children's comics; here 'The Dandy' is a fop. Half of BEANO is BEA, plus U.
explanation.definitionFit: A beau is a fashionable, well-dressed man, a fop, which is what a dandy is.

clue.text: Dressing fairly famous person with fake jewellery, covering one hand and the other

parts.note: a B-lister is a minor celebrity

indicators.note: covering means going over something, so one piece encloses another

parts.note: paste is glass used to imitate gems
L for left
R for right, the other hand

explanation.surface: A minor celebrity dressing up in fake jewels on both hands.
explanation.walkthrough: PASTE covers L to make PLASTE, then R completes PLASTER. A B-lister is a second-tier celebrity.
explanation.definitionFit: A blister plaster is an adhesive pad put over a blister, a kind of wound dressing.

clue.text: Recruit experienced, inspiring European Chancellor

indicators.note: inspiring is read as breathing in, so one letter is drawn inside

parts.note: to have had something is to have experienced it
E is the abbreviation for European
Jeremy Hunt was UK Chancellor of the Exchequer when this appeared

explanation.surface: An experienced pro-European Chancellor brings in new staff.
explanation.walkthrough: HAD breathes in E to give HEAD, then HUNT. The Chancellor of the Exchequer is the UK finance minister.
explanation.definitionFit: To headhunt is to approach and recruit someone already employed elsewhere for a job.

clue.text: Distance displayed by daughter accompanying escorts

indicators.note: escorting someone means walking either side of them, so one piece surrounds another

parts.note: with means accompanying
D is the abbreviation for daughter

explanation.surface: A daughter keeping her distance from the men taking her out.
explanation.walkthrough: WITH escorts D: WI(D)TH.
explanation.definitionFit: Width is a measurement across something, a distance from one side to the other.
